clue.text: Not so even in good or bad description?

parts.note: the prefix un- negates, so 'not' gives UN
more even, more level, is flatter

explanation.surface: A riddle about whether a description that is not even-handed counts as good or bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so even' reads as a comment on fairness, but it is UN plus FLATTER (more level); 'in good' then gives IN and G.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad description of someone is one that fails to compliment them, the opposite of flattery.

clue.text: Active peacekeepers initially collapse

indicators.note: initially says the peacekeepers come at the start, before the word for active

parts.note: UN peacekeepers are United Nations troops
someone active is doing things

explanation.surface: Peacekeeping troops in action at the start of a collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' puts UN first, ahead of DOING.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's undoing is their downfall or ruin, a collapse.

clue.text: Pert fellow's cheek

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
lip is insolence, as in 'don't give me any lip'

explanation.surface: A cheeky fellow being impudent.
explanation.definitionFit: Flip is short for flippant, meaning saucy or impertinent.

clue.text: Gave in wrong name for one from Anjou

indicators.note: wrong says the letters of 'gave in' plus N are set in a different, incorrect order

explanation.surface: Someone surrendered and was given the wrong name for a native of Anjou.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' rearranges GAVEIN with N added.
explanation.definitionFit: Angevin is the adjective and noun for a native of Anjou, the French region of the Plantagenet kings.

clue.text: It's not democratic, as a rule

explanation.surface: A system that is not democratic, as a general rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' looks like the everyday phrase 'usually', but the word 'rule' is the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyranny is absolute despotic government, the opposite of democracy, and is a kind of rule by one person.

clue.text: What you'd expect to get money for, when old?

definitions.text: What you'd expect to get money for, when old?

parts.words: What you'd expect to get money for, when old?
parts.note: plays on the idiom 'money for old ...', meaning easy money for no real work

explanation.surface: A question about what a pensioner might expect to be paid for.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'money for old rope' means pay for something requiring no effort.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names cordage as the worthless thing you are paid for, so the clue completes the saying.

clue.text: Marine creatures round a small island

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Marine creatures round a small island' (7): no parse of 'round a small island' gives the letters of NAUTILI, and a search of the exact text found no reprint; a word is likely misread or missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: Marine creatures round a small island

clue.text: Manufacturer is tense after river test

indicators.note: after says the words 'is tense' follow the river and test pieces

parts.note: the Indus is a great river of Pakistan
a trial is a test
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A manufacturer is nervous after a test on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like nervous, but it is T, the grammar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An industrialist owns or runs a manufacturing business.

clue.text: Endlessly irate foreigner improbably keeping cool

indicators.note: improbably says the letters are arranged in an unlikely new way
endlessly says the last letter of the word irate is cut off

explanation.surface: A furious foreigner is unlikely to be keeping calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' trims 'irate' to IRAT; 'improbably' rearranges IRAT plus FOREIGNER.
explanation.definitionFit: Refrigeration is the process of keeping things chilled.

clue.text: Showing agreement when dozing off

explanation.surface: Someone appears to agree in a meeting while actually falling asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving the head up and down signals assent, and the same motion happens when a drowsy head drops.

clue.text: Break up truer potential

indicators.note: potential suggests the letters could become something else, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: Breaking up a truer potential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potential' rearranges UPTRUER.
explanation.definitionFit: A rupture is a breach or split.

clue.text: Group of soldiers using some munitions

indicators.note: some says only a portion of the following word is taken, a run inside it

explanation.surface: A squad using part of the ammunition supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Using some' picks the letters inside 'munitions'.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is an organised military group, such as a company or battalion.

clue.text: Woman to join partnership? It's a fair bet

parts.note: Eve is the first woman in Genesis
North-South is a bridge partnership, abbreviated NS

explanation.surface: A woman joins a partnership, and the odds look good.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, North and South play as partners, so NS is a partnership.
explanation.definitionFit: A wager at even money pays the stake back once, a fair even chance.

clue.text: Late transport that is covered by railways, as before

indicators.note: covered by says the letters for 'that is' sit inside those for the railways

parts.note: BR is British Railways, the old name of the UK rail network

explanation.surface: A train service, protected by the railways as in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means dead: a bier carries a coffin. BR stood for British Rail, the former UK state railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A bier is the stand on which a coffin or corpse is carried, transport for the deceased.

clue.text: Collection initially tucked into receptacle

indicators.note: into says the opening letter goes inside the word for receptacle

parts.note: a sack is a bag, a receptacle

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the word tucked

explanation.surface: A collection is first put into a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A stack is a pile or heap, a collection of things.

clue.text: Fashion designer shows some sparkle, indeed

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A couturier's work has a certain glitter.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Klein is an American fashion designer.

clue.text: Hit gent unjustly, and increase tension

indicators.note: unjustly suggests something done wrongly, so the letters are put in a wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone strikes a gentleman without cause and makes things more tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unjustly' rearranges HITGENT.
explanation.definitionFit: To tighten a rope or spring is to make it more taut.

clue.text: Almost shout at noise of bullet, making doggy sound

indicators.note: almost says the word for shout loses its last letter

parts.note: to yell is to shout
a ricocheting bullet makes a ping

explanation.surface: Someone nearly shouts at a bullet's sound, like a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts YELL to YEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A yelp is the short shrill cry of a dog.

clue.text: Bad one taking cut from city — it's not legal

parts.note: ill means bad, as in ill will
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: cut from says the word city loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A bad one cuts loose from the city, breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut from' trims 'city' to CIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illicit is forbidden by law or custom.

clue.text: Seductive woman learning to put on garland

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting one piece on another places it above, so the learning comes first

parts.note: lore is traditional learning or knowledge
a lei is a Hawaiian flower garland

explanation.surface: A temptress learns to wear a garland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lorelei is the Rhine siren whose song lured boatmen to their death.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei of German legend is a siren, so the name stands for any temptress.

clue.text: Decline like Manx cat?

explanation.surface: A question about how a tailless cat comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Manx cat, from the Isle of Man, is born without a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A falling-away or dwindling is a decline; a Manx cat has its rear appendage missing.

clue.text: Mangle wife's caller?

parts.note: a ringer is someone who rings, a caller

explanation.surface: Asking about a wife's telephone caller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mangle' is the old laundry device with rollers, not the verb to wreck.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangle is a machine that squeezes water out of washing between rollers.

clue.text: A wretch travestied in The Observer?

indicators.note: travestied means grotesquely distorted, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A wretched person is mocked in The Observer newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travestied' rearranges AWRETCH. The Observer reads as the British Sunday newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: An observer is someone who looks on, a spectator.

clue.text: Expression of satisfaction unheard of from curate?

definitions.text: Expression of satisfaction unheard of from curate?

parts.words: Expression of satisfaction unheard of from curate?
parts.note: an old exclamation of approval, which the curate in the famous Punch cartoon never says because his egg was only good in parts

explanation.surface: A clergyman who never expresses satisfaction.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'curate's egg' is something good only in parts, from a Punch cartoon where a curate politely calls a bad egg 'good in parts'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was once a cheerful cry of approval, and its opposite is the partly bad egg of the curate.

clue.text: Latin joining boat for frolic

parts.note: Noah's ark is a boat

explanation.surface: A Latin speaker boards a boat for some fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is a bit of fun or a prank.

clue.text: Interval's final form?

explanation.surface: Asking about the last shape of an interval.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools the sixth form is the final two years before university.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, a sixth is the interval spanning six notes; the top school year is the sixth form.

clue.text: Slipper being thus, on foot?

indicators.note: on says the word for thus sits before the abbreviation for foot

parts.note: so means thus, as in 'do it so'

explanation.surface: A question about how a slipper feels when worn.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipper is a gentle, cushioned shoe, so on the foot it feels yielding.

clue.text: Charge about right? Then it won't be this

indicators.note: about says the word for charge goes round the letter for right

parts.note: a fee is a charge

explanation.surface: Is the charge about right? Then it won't cost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: If there is a charge at all, the item cannot be costless, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something costing nothing is gratis; once a charge is made, it is not.

clue.text: Mother joining team in a long skirt

parts.note: ma is mother
XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team

explanation.surface: A mother joins a team wearing a long skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A maxi is a skirt or dress reaching the ankles.

clue.text: Place New Orleans

indicators.note: new says the letters of Orleans are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Naming the city of New Orleans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Orleans' looks like a single place name, but 'New' rearranges ORLEANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Salerno is a port city in southern Italy.

clue.text: Sailor's call to lift dismissal

explanation.surface: A sailor's shout to raise something, and a sacking.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors chant it while hauling ropes; to be given 'the heave-ho' is to be fired or rejected.

clue.text: In which you might have beef about the crops?

definitions.text: In which you might have beef about the crops?

parts.words: In which you might have beef about the crops?
parts.note: beef reads as a complaint about crops, but it means beef cattle kept around arable fields on one farm

explanation.surface: Someone complaining about the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' looks like a grievance; it is cattle raised alongside crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Agriculture combining livestock with arable crops on the same holding.
